generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, the three moves run as one preparation for a single talk, whether it is a lab study, a coaching session plan or a case presentation. You read the brief to see what the format rewards, build a structure and visual aids that fit it, then rehearse and check for the common errors before the day. Run as one practice, each move feeds the next, so the sport science you present lands clearly.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two sport and exercise science students prepare the same assessed presentation on a study. Tom treats each stage alone: slides first, the brief read late, and no rehearsal. Amara runs the three moves as one practice, reading the brief, building a fitting structure, then rehearsing and trimming a crowded data slide for the common errors. Amara's talk fits the task and holds the room, because the moves worked together.
generatedProse.summary: Across your presentations in the School of Sport, these three moves are strongest run as one practice. Read the brief, build a fitting structure and visual aids, then rehearse and correct the common errors before the day. It is the practice, repeated, that makes your delivery reliable.

check.body: A student reads the brief for a poster, designs a clear visual layout to fit it, rehearses the two-minute summary to time, and trims a crowded panel before the day. What does this show?

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following programme improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next programme, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next programme improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.
